title: Diagnostic misdirection in posterior-onset Rasmussen's encephalitis: A case report
case_prompt:
An 11-year-old boy with no personal or family history of epilepsy began at age 6 with brief (seconds to 2 minutes) stereotyped episodes of seeing colorful objects in the left visual field, accompanied by pallor, headache, and hypersomnolence. Valproic acid was initiated, and these events remained isolated for one year. At age 7, he had a left hemibody tonic-clonic seizure with postictal weakness, leading to the addition of levetiracetam. By age 9, he developed weekly episodes characterized by visual hallucinations followed by impaired awareness, oral and manual automatisms, left hemibody dystonia, and occasional secondary generalization, accompanied by psychomotor regression and declining school performance. A brain MRI at that time was normal, and clobazam was added. Over the next two years, seizures continued twice weekly despite therapy with carbamazepine, levetiracetam, and clobazam. 

On examination in November 2023, he was alert and interactive. Neurological evaluation revealed mild left hemiparesis and asymmetry of muscle tone, without sensory deficits or reflex asymmetry. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 1 WBC/mm3 and normal glucose, protein, and lactate. Thyroid function tests, antinuclear antibody screening, complement levels, viral serologies for VZV, CMV, hepatitis B and C, and onconeural markers were all within normal limits or negative. 

Interictal EEG demonstrated repetitive slow-wave discharges originating in the right occipital region and spreading ipsilaterally. Perictal EEG showed occipital background slowing with diffuse delta activity progressing centrally, followed by rhythmic acceleration. A repeat brain MRI revealed marked right hemispheric atrophy. FDG-PET demonstrated diffuse hypometabolism throughout the right frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes and ipsilateral basal ganglia.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious encephalitis was considered but excluded — “Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 1 WBC/mm3 with normal glucose, protein, and lactate levels … viral serologies (VZV, CMV, hepatitis B and C) [were normal].”  
2. Autoimmune or systemic inflammatory encephalitis was considered but excluded — “autoimmune antibody screening (antinuclear antibody), complement levels … were normal.”  
3. Paraneoplastic encephalitis was considered but excluded — “Onconeural markers were also negative.”  
4. Small-vessel CNS vasculitis was considered but excluded — “Differential diagnoses, including other causes of encephalitis, small vessel CNS vasculitis, and systemic inflammatory conditions with CNS involvement, were excluded.”
